title: Balancing estimators in synthetic panels
text:
1 Overview
This study compares estimators of the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) in five synthetic panel families: classic factors, weak factors, mixed factors, sparse synthetic controls, and autoregressive outcomes. Each canonical panel contains 160 never-treated units, 40 treated units, 40 pre-treatment periods, and 10 post-treatment periods. All treated units adopt in the first post-treatment period. Their treatment effects increase from 0.2 to 2.0, which gives a true ATT of 1.1.
The estimators reconstruct untreated post-treatment outcomes in three ways. An outcome-model estimator uses a fitted untreated-outcome surface. Unit balancing weights control units so their pre-treatment outcomes match the treated units. Double balancing combines those donor weights with weights on pre-treatment periods in an augmented difference-in-differences score. The experiments vary factor-loading overlap, factor strength, donor sparsity, persistence, and integration to change which source of information is useful. For copyable construction code and matshow visualizations of every underlying design, start with the Balancing DGP catalog.
The estimator ranking changes across these designs. Unit balancing is competitive in several good-overlap and synthetic-control settings. Double balancing has substantially lower RMSE under poor factor-loading overlap and persistent integrated dynamics. No outcome model or balancing configuration minimizes RMSE in every design.
The reproduction uses three validation standards:

On the same fixed panel, the R quadratic-program reference and crabbymetrics.AugmentedBalancing agree to numerical precision across 48 estimator configurations.
On a second fixed panel, Python FE, IFE, MCPanel, generalized synthetic-control, and panel-VAR surfaces agree with their R reference surfaces within specified cell tolerances.
Independent R and Python Monte Carlo runs compare the full 398-cell slide grid. Differences are reported in units of combined Monte Carlo standard errors.

Of the 398 Monte Carlo cells, 390 are within three combined Monte Carlo standard errors. Every FE, IFE, generalized synthetic-control, and VAR cell is within that boundary. The eight exceptions consist of five correlated MCPanel cells in the poor-overlap classic-factor setting and three ARIMA cells in the low-persistence time-series settings. These two outcome-model-specific patterns are documented below.

2 Sources and implementation contracts
The visual reference is drafts/slides.pdf, with source in overleaf_v2/acic_2024_deck.tex. The executable contracts come from:

code/ziyi/formal simulation DGP.R for panel generation;
code/ziyi/classic_did_framework.R for estimator composition;
code/ziyi/support/sdid_unit.R and sdid_time.R for ridge balancing;
code/ziyi/support/scm.R for the penalized-SCM donor loss;
output/simulation/*/estimation.RData for the exact slide Monte Carlo draws; and
code/apoorva/00_acic_tabfig.R for the slide aggregation rule, \(\operatorname{RMSE}=\sqrt{\operatorname{mean}(\widehat\tau-\tau)^2}\).

The reproduced ATT heatmaps appear on deck pages 27-28 for classic factors, 33-36 for synthetic controls, 41-44 for time series, 48-49 for weak factors, and 54-55 for mixed factors.
The Python comparison is exact for the balancing estimator and its penalties. It also implements all outcome-model columns in the R heatmaps: FE, IFE, MCPanel, generalized synthetic control, panel VAR, and the time-series-only ARIMA column. The Monte Carlo comparison uses the same probability laws and replication indices 1 through 200, but NumPy and R do not use the same seeded random streams. Therefore, Monte Carlo equality is evaluated relative to simulation uncertainty, not bitwise equality.
Several details in the executable R source determine the numerical results:








Component
Executable R contract
Why it matters




Factor scale
Divide each realized factor path by its sample SD
Fixes the realized signal scale and signal-to-noise ratio


Synthetic donors
Sample active donors without replacement with weights 1 for favored donors and 0.1 for other donors
Changes the donor support in each replication


Time-series mean
Set the treated innovation mean to 0.25
Separates the innovation mean from the unconditional AR level mean


Mixed factors
Generate two half-panels and restart the seed for the second half
Preserves the dependence structure of the archived experiment


Unit balancing
Use optimized unit weights and uniform pre-period weights in the augmented score
Retains the time correction when time weights are not optimized


Period targets
Fit one time-weight vector for each post period
Allows the time target to change over the post-treatment path


IFE controls
Rank 2 and force 3; tolerance \(10^{-5}\) for classic and weak factors and \(10^{-4}\) otherwise
Matches the archived fect calls


MCPanel
Unit and time effects with fixed nuclear-norm penalty 0.002
Matches lambda_L=0.002 with cross-validation disabled


Panel VAR
Use 2 lags for classic and weak factors, 1 for mixed factors and SCM, and 4 for time-series panels
The archived scripts do not use one common lag order


ARIMA
Fit an automatic univariate time-series model to each unit
This column appears only in the time-series DGP


Monte Carlo size
Use 200 successful replications per cell
Makes the reported RMSE comparable to the archived R experiment



These are part of the statistical specification. They are not interchangeable implementation details.

3 Exact same-panel estimator parity
The fixture generator in crabbymetrics/tests/fixtures/generate_r_augmented_balancing_reference.R uses R and quadprog to fit all combinations of:

balance: unit, time, or double;
unit_target: cohort or individual;
time_target: all post periods or one post period at a time;
balance_on: raw outcomes or outcome-model residuals; and
unit_loss: SDID ridge or penalized SCM.

The following code sends the identical panel and outcome-model surface to Python.

4 R and Python Monte Carlo results

4.1 Plot construction
Each row below contains the complete R heatmap and the complete Python heatmap for one setting. The two panels have the same rows, columns, blanks, and color scale. The slide aggregation leaves unit-only and unaugmented double balancing blank outside the FE column because those two estimators do not use an outcome model.
Color follows the slide rule: direct RMSE from 0 to 3 on the reversed Spectral palette. Values above 3 and unavailable cells are gray. Printed labels retain the uncensored RMSE values.


Show code
def _matrix_for(data, setting, outcomes):
    selected = data[data["setting"].eq(setting)]
    matrix = (
        selected.pivot_table(index="frame", columns="outcome", values="rmse", aggfunc="first")
        .reindex(index=FRAME_ORDER, columns=outcomes)
    )
    matrix.loc[["u-balance", "d-balance"], [name for name in outcomes if name != "fe"]] = np.nan
    return matrix


def _draw_heatmap(ax, matrix, title, *, show_y=True):
    values = matrix.to_numpy(dtype=float)
    color_values = np.ma.masked_where(
        ~np.isfinite(values) | (values < 0) | (values > 3),
        values,
    )
    palette = mpl.colormaps["Spectral_r"].copy()
    palette.set_bad("#8c8c8c")
    image = ax.imshow(
        color_values,
        aspect="auto",
        cmap=palette,
        vmin=0,
        vmax=3,
    )
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10, loc="left")
    ax.set_xticks(range(matrix.shape[1]), matrix.columns, rotation=35, ha="right")
    if show_y:
        ax.set_yticks(range(matrix.shape[0]), matrix.index)
    else:
        ax.set_yticks(range(matrix.shape[0]), [])
    for row in range(values.shape[0]):
        for column in range(values.shape[1]):
            value = values[row, column]
            if np.isfinite(value):
                ax.text(column, row, f"{value:.3g}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)
    return image


def plot_family(family, settings, title):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        len(settings),
        2,
        figsize=(15.5, max(3.4, 3.2 * len(settings))),
        gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1]},
        squeeze=False,
        constrained_layout=True,
    )
    for row, setting in enumerate(settings):
        r_setting = r_results[(r_results["family"] == family) & (r_results["setting"] == setting)]
        available = [name for name in OUTCOME_ORDER if name in set(r_setting["outcome"])]
        r_full = _matrix_for(r_setting, setting, available)
        p_setting = python_results[
            (python_results["family"] == family) & (python_results["setting"] == setting)
        ]
        p_full = _matrix_for(p_setting, setting, available)
        image = _draw_heatmap(
            axes[row, 0],
            r_full,
            f"R reference | {setting}",
            show_y=True,
        )
        _draw_heatmap(
            axes[row, 1],
            p_full,
            f"Python reproduction | {setting}",
            show_y=False,
        )
    fig.colorbar(
        image,
        ax=axes,
        orientation="horizontal",
        fraction=0.025,
        pad=0.08,
        label="RMSE (values above 3 are gray)",
    )
    fig.suptitle(title, fontsize=14)
    plt.show()

5 Between-language Monte Carlo agreement
For independent Monte Carlo estimates \(\widehat r_R\) and \(\widehat r_P\), define
\[
z_{R-P}=\frac{\widehat r_P-\widehat r_R}
{\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\widehat r_P)^2+
\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\widehat r_R)^2}}.
\]
For errors \(e_s\) and \(r=\sqrt{S^{-1}\sum_s e_s^2}\), the delta-method standard error used here is
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(r)=
\frac{\operatorname{sd}(e_s^2)}{2r\sqrt{S}}.
\]

5.1 Discrepancy diagnosis
The same-panel checks identify the source of a difference before the Monte Carlo results are interpreted:

FE, IFE, generalized synthetic control, and panel VAR agree cell by cell to \(10^{-8}\). A Monte Carlo difference in these columns is not an estimator-algebra difference.
MCPanel agrees to \(5\times10^{-4}\) on the fixed panel. Its remaining numerical difference comes from the stopping sequence used by the Rcpp and Rust SVD routines.
ARIMA does not have a same-panel historical-fable fixture. The Python search contains the true DGP models but searches fewer ARMA specifications than fable::ARIMA. A persistent ARIMA-column difference is therefore an outcome-model search difference.
The R and Python simulations use independent random streams. The standardized difference accounts for the reported Monte Carlo error from both runs.
Cells in one setting reuse the same 200 panels. Their standardized differences are correlated, so a cluster of adjacent cells is one setting-level diagnostic rather than a set of independent tests.

A standardized difference near zero is expected under the common probability law. The two tables above show both the most extreme cells and the outcome-model-level pattern. This makes a package-algorithm difference visible instead of attributing every difference to random simulation noise.

Use:

model.fit(y, w, outcome_model=None)

y is a finite balanced outcome matrix with units in rows and periods in columns.
w is a same-shaped binary absorbing-treatment matrix.
outcome_model is an optional same-shaped untreated-outcome surface fitted without treated post-treatment outcomes. If omitted, it is zero.

All three arrays must be two-dimensional. y and outcome_model must be finite. w must be binary and absorbing. Each treated cohort must have at least one pre-treatment period, and the panel must contain a never-treated donor. Invalid constructor choices, invalid arrays, unsupported treatment paths, and solver failures raise ValueError. predict(), treatment_effect(), and summary() raise ValueError before a successful fit.


8.2 Counterfactual formula
Let \(C\) be never-treated controls, \(P\) be pre-treatment periods, and \(\hat m\) be the supplied outcome model. Define residuals \(R=Y-\hat m\). For treated unit \(i\) and post period \(t\),
\[
\widehat Y_{it}(0)
=
\hat m_{it}
+\sum_{j\in C}\hat\omega_jR_{jt}
+\sum_{s\in P}\hat\lambda_sR_{is}
-\sum_{j\in C}\sum_{s\in P}\hat\omega_j\hat\lambda_sR_{js}.
\]
The balance choice controls which weights are optimized:



balance
Unit weights \(\omega\)
Time weights \(\lambda\)




"none"
Not used
Not used; returns \(\hat m\)


"unit"
Optimized
Uniform over pre periods


"time"
Uniform over controls
Optimized


"double"
Optimized
Optimized



With balance="unit", the estimator retains the time correction and uses uniform pre-period weights.


8.3 Targets

unit_target="cohort" fits one donor vector to the treated-cohort mean.
unit_target="individual" fits one donor vector per treated unit.
time_target="all" fits one pre-period vector to the control post-period mean.
time_target="period" fits one pre-period vector for each post period.

The R “individual double” row maps to unit_target="individual", time_target="period".


8.4 Weight-fitting data

balance_on="raw" fits weights with \(Y\).
balance_on="residual" fits weights with \(R=Y-\hat m\).

In both cases, the final augmentation formula is applied to residuals \(R\). balance_on changes the weight-fitting problem, not the final algebra.


8.5 Unit losses and penalties
unit_loss="ridge" implements the SDID simplex ridge problem with a profiled intercept. If zeta_omega and zeta_lambda are omitted, the R defaults are
\[
\zeta_\omega=(N_{\text{target}}T_{\text{post}})^{1/4}\hat\sigma,
\qquad
\zeta_\lambda=10^{-6}\hat\sigma,
\]
where \(\hat\sigma\) is the sample SD of control first differences in the selected balancing data. For individual unit targets, \(N_{\text{target}}=1\).
unit_loss="penalized_scm" implements penSCM from the R source. It standardizes the donor matrix by its sample SD and adds the linear donor-distance penalty. unit_penalty=1e-4 is the R default. Time weights remain SDID ridge weights.
The internal active-set solver handles simplex boundary solutions directly. It can represent exact zero weights, unlike a softmax parameterization.

title: Balancing estimators in synthetic panels
text:
10 Scope and limitations

Same-panel parity tests the numerical estimator implementation. It does not test random-number-generator parity.
The Monte Carlo comparison tests common probability laws with independent language-specific random streams. Differences are therefore evaluated with combined Monte Carlo standard errors.
The Monte Carlo comparison covers all 398 displayed R/Python cells. FE, IFE, MCPanel, generalized synthetic control, and VAR also have same-panel R parity fixtures. ARIMA has a Monte Carlo check but no historical-fable same-panel fixture in this environment.
The experiments compare point-estimator RMSE under a common-adoption design. They do not evaluate interval coverage, staggered adoption, or treatment-effect heterogeneity beyond the common linear post-treatment path.

title: Balancing estimators in synthetic panels
text:
11 Conclusions

Unit-only balancing is effective in several good-overlap and synthetic-control settings.
No single balancing or outcome-model configuration is uniformly best.
Double balancing materially reduces RMSE under poor factor-loading overlap and under persistent integrated dynamics.
Individual unit and post-period targets can help, but they are different estimators and require many more weight fits.
Outcome-model performance remains DGP-specific. The R and Python heatmaps show that gsynth, ife, MCPanel, VAR, and arima have different strengths. A horizontal-ridge result cannot stand in for those columns.

These conclusions rest on an exact same-panel R test, executable R DGP contracts, 200 successful draws in every Monte Carlo cell, and a between-language comparison scaled by combined Monte Carlo uncertainty.

3.1 BakerStateFeatures
Creates one observed integer feature named state. Following the source DGP, each unit independently samples a state ID from zero through n_states - 1. The state feature is included in PanelDataset.unit_covariates and the long interchange output.


3.2 BakerCohortAssignment
Randomly permutes states and divides them according to cohort_state_counts. Every unit in a state receives the same adoption period, and treatment is absorbing. Assignment metadata records the randomized state order and the cohort period for each state and unit.


3.3 BakerAdditiveOutcome
Generates
\[
Y_{it}(0) = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \varepsilon_{it},
\]
with independent centered Gaussian draws governed by the three configured scales. Metadata retains the realized unit effects, time effects, and error matrix.


3.4 BakerDynamicEffect
For a unit in cohort \(G_i=g\) with configured slope \(s_g\), the realized effect is
\[
\tau_{it} = \mathbb{1}\{t \geq g\}\,s_g\,(t-g+1)\,\texttt{effect_scale}.
\]
The first treated-period effect is therefore \(s_g\), not zero. Pre-treatment effects are exactly zero. Negative slopes are allowed, while effect_scale must be nonnegative.

title: Balancing DGP catalog
text:
This is the construction guide for the data-generating processes behind the balancing reproduction. That vignette answers how the estimators perform. This page answers the more basic question: what is each DGP, and how do I actually draw it with pypanelsim?
The report contains 12 statistically distinct settings across five DGP families. Its results contain 14 named cases because each of the two synthetic-control settings is fitted once with ridge unit balancing and once with penalized-SCM unit balancing. Those are estimator choices, not four different DGPs. The archived package also contains a sixth, factor–synthetic mixture, which was not used in the 398-cell comparison; it is documented and plotted here as well.

title: Balancing DGP catalog
text:
1 Setup and the shared experiment


Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pypanelsim as pps

config = pps.CanonicalPanelConfig(
    n_control=160,
    n_treated=40,
    n_pre=40,
    n_post=10,
    effect_slope=0.2,
    noise_variance=0.36,
)
config


CanonicalPanelConfig(n_control=160, n_treated=40, n_pre=40, n_post=10, effect_slope=0.2, noise_variance=0.36)


Every factory on this page uses that configuration by default. Thus each draw has 200 units by 50 periods. Units 0–159 are never treated; units 160–199 adopt at zero-based period 40. The treatment effect on every treated unit is the deterministic ramp
\[
\tau_{it}=0.2(t-39),\qquad t=40,\ldots,49,
\]
so treated-period effects run from 0.2 through 2.0 and the true ATT is 1.1. Independent observation noise has standard deviation 0.6. Only the untreated outcome law changes across the sections below.
There are two equivalent ways to use a canonical DGP. The *_design form returns a reusable simulator; the shorter form draws one panel immediately.


Code
# Reusable simulator: use this for Monte Carlo work.
simulator = pps.classic_factor_design(overlap=1.0, config=config)
panel_17 = simulator.simulate(seed=17)
panel_18 = simulator.simulate(seed=18)

# One-draw convenience function: same result for the same seed.
same_panel = pps.classic_factor(overlap=1.0, config=config, seed=17)
np.array_equal(panel_17.outcome, same_panel.outcome)


True


Each returned PanelDataset exposes (unit, time) arrays named outcome, treatment, untreated_outcome, and treatment_effect. The plots below put the observed outcome \(Y\) and assignment \(W\) side by side. The horizontal boundary separates controls from treated units; the vertical boundary is the common adoption date.


Show the plotting helper
def matshow_panels(draws, *, title, n_pre=config.n_pre):
    """Plot a sequence of (label, PanelDataset) pairs on a common Y scale."""
    scale = np.quantile(
        np.abs(np.concatenate([panel.outcome.ravel() for _, panel in draws])),
        0.98,
    )
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        len(draws),
        2,
        figsize=(11.5, 2.45 * len(draws)),
        squeeze=False,
        constrained_layout=True,
    )
    for row, (label, panel) in enumerate(draws):
        treated_boundary = panel.control_units.size - 0.5
        y_axis, w_axis = axes[row]
        y_axis.matshow(
            panel.outcome,
            aspect="auto",
            cmap="RdBu_r",
            vmin=-scale,
            vmax=scale,
        )
        w_axis.matshow(
            panel.treatment,
            aspect="auto",
            cmap="Greys",
            vmin=0,
            vmax=1,
        )
        for axis in (y_axis, w_axis):
            axis.axvline(n_pre - 0.5, color="#f5a623", linewidth=1.2)
            axis.axhline(treated_boundary, color="#f5a623", linewidth=1.2)
            axis.xaxis.set_ticks_position("bottom")
            axis.set_xlabel("period")
        y_axis.set_ylabel(f"{label}\nunit")
        y_axis.set_title("Observed outcome Y")
        w_axis.set_title("Treatment W")
    fig.suptitle(title, fontsize=14)
    plt.show()

title: Balancing DGP catalog
text:
3 1. Classic factor
Use this design for an interactive-fixed-effects panel with two strong, drifting common factors:
\[
Y_{it}(0)=\lambda_i^\top f_t+\varepsilon_{it},
\qquad
\lambda_i\sim
\begin{cases}
N(-a,I_2),&i\text{ control},\\
N(a,I_2),&i\text{ treated}.
\end{cases}
\]
Each \(f_t\) is a standardized AR(1) path with coefficient 0.5 plus a linear drift \(0.5t\). overlap=0 gives the treated and control loadings the same distribution. overlap=1 moves their means to opposite sides of factor space, making the treated counterfactual harder to recover from controls.


Code
classic_draws = [
    ("a = 0: overlapping loadings", pps.classic_factor(overlap=0, seed=110)),
    ("a = 1: separated loadings", pps.classic_factor(overlap=1, seed=110)),
]
matshow_panels(classic_draws, title="Classic factor DGP")









The realized latent objects are available for diagnosis:

print("loadings:", classic.metadata["outcome"]["loadings"].shape)
print("factors:", classic.metadata["outcome"]["factors"].shape)

Use this to make the factor structure diffuse and individually weak. The law is again \(Y_{it}(0)=\lambda_i^\top f_t+\varepsilon_{it}\), but there are ten factors: five drifting paths and five cycles \(\sin(\pi t/15)\). Every standardized factor is multiplied by 0.2. The same overlap parameter controls the treated–control loading gap.

5 3. Mixed factor
Use this when one factor model is not shared by the whole population. The 200 units are split into two 100-unit blocks:

the first block contains 60 controls and all 40 treated units and follows two drift factors;
the second block contains 100 controls only and follows two cyclical factors.

The two blocks restart from the same RNG state, matching the archived implementation. overlap separates treated loadings from the controls in the first block. It does not turn overlap into a treatment-assignment probability.

title: Balancing DGP catalog
text:
6 4. Sparse synthetic control
Use this when treated counterfactuals are convex combinations of a sparse set of donors. Control outcomes first follow a two-drift-factor model. Let \(m=\lceil qN_0\rceil\), where q=active_share. Controls with the \(m\) largest loading scores get sampling weight 1 and all other controls get weight 0.1. Then \(m\) donors are sampled without replacement and receive equal convex weights:
\[
Y_{it}(0)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j\in\mathcal A}Y_{jt}^{\text{factor}}
+u_{it}+\varepsilon_{it},\qquad i\text{ treated}.
\]

7 5. Time series
Use this when independent unit dynamics, rather than shared factors or donors, generate untreated outcomes. For each unit,
\[
x_{it}=\phi x_{i,t-1}+\mu_i+\eta_{it},\qquad
\mu_i=0\ \text{for controls},\quad \mu_i=0.25\ \text{for treated units}.
\]
With integrated=False, \(Y_{it}(0)=x_{it}+\varepsilon_{it}\). With integrated=True, \(Y_{it}(0)=\sum_{s\leq t}x_{is}+\varepsilon_{it}\), an ARIMA(1,1,0)-type path. The report crosses low or high persistence coefficient=0.2, 0.9 with stationary or integrated paths.

8 6. Factor–synthetic mixture
This archived design is useful even though it is not one of the 12 unique settings in the final balancing grid. It forms one drift factor and one cyclical factor, constructs a synthetic component using 40 active donors, and then mixes the two signals equally:
\[
Y_{it}(0)=0.5Y_{it}^{\text{factor}}+0.5Y_{it}^{\text{SCM}}
+\varepsilon_{it}.
\]
The treated-specific noise in the SCM component has standard deviation 2. overlap controls factor-loading separation exactly as in the other factor designs.

title: Assignment mechanisms
text:
Assignment and untreated outcomes often depend on the same unit attributes. UnitFeatureModel draws these attributes before assignment and splits them into:

observables, exposed as panel.unit_covariates; and
unobservables, retained under panel.metadata["features"] as simulation truth.

GaussianUnitFeatures(k_x, k_u) supplies independent standard-normal features. A custom feature model can instead introduce correlation, discrete covariates, or application-specific population structure.


Code
from dataclasses import dataclass

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pypanelsim as pps


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class FeatureOutcome:
    def generate(self, context, rng):
        t = np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, context.dimensions.n_periods)
        factor = np.sin(np.linspace(0.0, 3.0 * np.pi, context.dimensions.n_periods))
        y0 = (
            0.8 * context.observables[:, :1]
            + 0.6 * context.observables[:, 1:2] * t
            + 1.2 * context.unobservables[:, :1] * (t + 1.0)
            + 0.8 * context.unobservables[:, 1:2] * factor
        )
        y0 += rng.normal(scale=0.35, size=y0.shape)
        return pps.ComponentDraw(y0, {"kind": "feature_outcome"})


dimensions = pps.PanelDimensions(120, 48)
features = pps.GaussianUnitFeatures(2, 2)


def build(name, assignment):
    return pps.PanelSimulator(
        name=name,
        dimensions=dimensions,
        feature_model=features,
        assignment=assignment,
        outcome_model=FeatureOutcome(),
        effect_model=pps.LinearRampEffect(0.12),
    )

RandomizedSingleCohortAssignment samples exactly n_treated eligible units without replacement. Every eligible unit has marginal treatment probability n_treated / n_eligible; ineligible units have probability zero.

title: Assignment mechanisms
text:
3 Binary logit selection
BinaryLogitAssignment independently draws eventual treatment from
\[
e_i=P(D_i=1\mid X_i,U_i)
=\Lambda\!\left(\alpha+X_i^\top\beta+U_i^\top\gamma\right),
\]
where \(\Lambda(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\). The selected units adopt at one common period. The assignment metadata records every linear predictor and propensity score.

3.1 Selection on observables
Set \(\gamma=0\):


Code
observed_selection = build(
    "observed_selection",
    pps.BinaryLogitAssignment(
        adoption_period=32,
        intercept=-1.1,
        observable_coefficients=(1.2, -0.8),
        unobservable_coefficients=(0.0, 0.0),
    ),
)
observed_panel = observed_selection.simulate(seed=2026)
print(observed_panel.unit_covariate_names)
print(observed_panel.metadata["assignment"]["propensity_scores"][:5])


('x1', 'x2')
[0.09585059 0.01107192 0.47491899 0.1522054  0.22435501]


When the potential-outcome law also depends on \(X\) but treatment does not depend on \(U\), assignment is unconfounded conditional on the exposed covariates. The unadjusted treated and control groups need not be comparable.


3.2 Selection on latent factors
Set \(\beta=0\) and \(\gamma\ne0\):


Code
latent_selection = build(
    "latent_selection",
    pps.BinaryLogitAssignment(
        adoption_period=32,
        intercept=-1.1,
        observable_coefficients=(0.0, 0.0),
        unobservable_coefficients=(1.4, -1.0),
    ),
)
latent_panel = latent_selection.simulate(seed=2026)
print(latent_panel.metadata["features"]["unobservables"].shape)


(120, 2)


This assignment is confounded relative to estimators that see only \(X\). Panel factor, matrix-completion, trajectory-balancing, and synthetic-control methods may nevertheless learn part of the latent structure from pre-treatment paths. How well they do is an estimand- and DGP-specific numerical question.

title: Assignment mechanisms
text:
4 Adoption-cohort generalized propensity scores
For adoption periods \(g\in\mathcal G\), GeneralizedPropensityAssignment uses the multinomial-logit generalized propensity score
\[
r_g(X_i,U_i)=P(G_i=g\mid X_i,U_i)
=\frac{\exp(\alpha_g+X_i^\top\beta_g+U_i^\top\gamma_g)}
{1+\sum_{h\in\mathcal G}\exp(\alpha_h+X_i^\top\beta_h+U_i^\top\gamma_h)}.
\]
Never treated is the baseline category with normalized logit zero. Each sampled cohort produces absorbing treatment from its adoption period onward.


Code
cohort_gps = build(
    "cohort_gps",
    pps.GeneralizedPropensityAssignment(
        adoption_periods=(24, 30, 36),
        intercepts=(-0.7, -0.9, -1.1),
        observable_coefficients=(
            (1.0, -0.5),
            (0.2, 0.8),
            (-0.8, 0.3),
        ),
        unobservable_coefficients=((0.0, 0.0),) * 3,
    ),
)
cohort_panel = cohort_gps.simulate(seed=2026)
gps = cohort_panel.metadata["assignment"]["generalized_propensity_scores"]
print(gps.shape)
print(np.max(np.abs(gps.sum(axis=1) - 1.0)))
print(np.unique(cohort_panel.adoption_times, return_counts=True))


(120, 4)
2.220446049250313e-16
(array([24, 30, 36, 48]), array([26, 22, 28, 44]))


Metadata includes generalized_propensity_scores, assigned_categories, adoption_times, cohort logits, coefficient matrices, and the never-treated category index.

title: Assignment mechanisms
text:
5 Heterogeneous treatment effects
The effect input may be a lambda defining a unit-level effect
\[
\tau_i=f(X_i,U_i).
\]
The lambda receives SimulationContext, so the same observed covariates and latent factors used by assignment and untreated outcomes are available as x.observables and x.unobservables. It returns either a scalar or one value per unit. PanelSimulator broadcasts the resulting \(\tau_i\) over time and multiplies it by realized treatment.


Code
heterogeneous = pps.PanelSimulator(
    name="heterogeneous_effects",
    dimensions=dimensions,
    feature_model=features,
    assignment=pps.RandomizedSingleCohortAssignment(
        n_treated=40,
        adoption_period=32,
    ),
    outcome_model=FeatureOutcome(),
    effect_model=lambda x: (
        1.0

        - 0.30 * x.observables[:, 1]

title: 1 Architecture and extension contract
text:
PanelSimulator evaluates components in a fixed order:
PanelDimensions
      |
      v
UnitFeatureModel.generate(dimensions, rng) [optional]
      |
      v
AssignmentContext(dimensions, observables, unobservables)
      |
      v
AssignmentModel.assign(context, rng)
      |
      v
SimulationContext(dimensions, treatment, features)
      |
      +-------------------------+
      |                         |
      v                         v
OutcomeModel.generate()   EffectModel.generate()
      |                         |
      +------------+------------+
                   |
                   v
              PanelDataset
Shared unit features are drawn before assignment. This lets an assignment and an outcome process depend on the same observed covariates or latent unit factors without passing data through diagnostic metadata. Assignment still precedes the outcome draw, and the untreated outcome model does not receive realized effects. The effect model does not receive outcomes. This keeps the causal decomposition explicit.





PanelDimensions(n_units, n_periods) defines only shape. It does not assume a control-first unit order, one treatment cohort, or a specific intervention date.



Every component returns ComponentDraw(values, metadata). values must be a matrix with the configured shape. Metadata can contain diagnostics or latent simulation truth. The final dataset copies and recursively freezes metadata.



The assignment context contains dimensions, observed unit covariates, and latent unit features. Its matrices have shape (n_units, n_features). The feature model is optional, so legacy and canonical assignments receive empty feature matrices without consuming additional random draws.



The context contains dimensions, realized treatment, and the same features used by assignment. It derives:

ever_treated;
control_units;
treated_units;
is_absorbing;
adoption_times for absorbing treatment.

Outcome models can therefore depend on treatment status without assuming that controls appear before treated units.



The dataset owns the final arrays. It validates shape, finiteness, binary treatment, effect support, and the causal decomposition. Its read-only arrays are safe to share among estimators. copy=True creates writable estimator inputs when required. Observed time-invariant covariates are available through unit_covariates; latent features remain namespaced simulation metadata.




The component interfaces use typing.Protocol. Inheritance is optional.
class UnitFeatureModel(Protocol):
    def generate(self, dimensions, rng) -> UnitFeatureDraw: ...


class AssignmentModel(Protocol):
    def assign(self, context, rng) -> ComponentDraw: ...


class OutcomeModel(Protocol):
    def generate(self, context, rng) -> ComponentDraw: ...


class EffectModel(Protocol):
    def generate(self, context, rng) -> ComponentDraw: ...
The package validates the returned matrices at the composition boundary. A custom class can focus on its probability law.



PanelSimulator.simulate() resolves one numpy.random.Generator. Components receive the same generator in pipeline order. A deterministic component should not consume random draws.
Accepted inputs are:

seed=<integer>;
seed=<numpy.random.SeedSequence>;
rng=<numpy.random.Generator>;
neither, for a fresh entropy-seeded generator.

Passing both is an error. iter_simulations() uses SeedSequence.spawn() to create independent child streams instead of using adjacent integer seeds.
When a design needs two components to restart from the same state, it must clone the generator explicitly and document that choice. The canonical mixed-factor design does this because it reproduces two half-panels that restart from the same random stream.






SingleCohortAssignment creates one absorbing cohort. It supports explicit treated-unit positions.
StaggeredAdoption accepts a mapping from unit position to adoption period.
RandomizedSingleCohortAssignment samples a fixed-size cohort without replacement.
BinaryLogitAssignment draws treatment from observed and latent unit-feature logits.
GeneralizedPropensityAssignment draws adoption cohorts from multinomial logits with never treated as the baseline category.





GaussianUnitFeatures draws independent standard-normal observed covariates and latent unit factors. Custom feature models can impose correlations or generate application-specific covariates.





ConstantEffect applies one effect to every treated cell.
LinearRampEffect uses unit-specific event time and supports staggered adoption.
CallableUnitEffect evaluates a scalar or unit-vector law against the shared SimulationContext; PanelSimulator automatically wraps a lambda passed as effect_model.




CallableOutcomeModel turns a function into an outcome component. The function can return a matrix or a ComponentDraw with metadata.





Define an immutable configuration object, normally a frozen dataclass.
Validate scalar parameters in __post_init__.
Implement the relevant protocol method.
Use only the provided generator for random draws.
Return a full (n_units, n_periods) matrix.
Put diagnostic truth in metadata, not global state.
Add contract, invalid-input, and seeded-reproducibility tests.

An outcome model should use context.control_units and context.treated_units rather than assume a row order. An effect model must return zero outside treated cells.



Write a factory that returns a configured PanelSimulator:
def unit_trend_design(*, scale=1.0):
    return PanelSimulator(
        name="unit_trend",
        dimensions=PanelDimensions(100, 30),
        assignment=SingleCohortAssignment(20, 20),
        outcome_model=UnitTrendOutcome(scale=scale),
        effect_model=ConstantEffect(1.0),
    )
Register it in a project registry:
registry = DGPRegistry()
registry.register("unit_trend", unit_trend_design)
Do not add estimator options to a simulation factory. Estimator configuration belongs in the downstream experiment runner.



The dataset copies arrays before setting them read-only. Mutating an input array after construction cannot change the dataset. Nested mappings, arrays, lists, and sets in metadata are also copied or converted to immutable forms.
The package does not promise that arbitrary scalar objects inside metadata are deeply immutable. Store simple scalars, arrays, mappings, and sequences.



The current PanelDataset contract requires a balanced rectangular panel and binary treatment. Missing outcomes can be represented by a separate custom metadata mask, but the core outcome matrices must remain finite. A future missing-data extension should add an explicit observation mask instead of using NaN as an implicit contract.

The former dgps project mixed simulation code with crabbymetrics outcome models, Monte Carlo runners, cached results, and a Quarto report. pypanelsim contains only simulation code and simulation documentation. # Current

    n_control=80,
    n_treated=20,
    n_pre=24,
    n_post=6,
)
panel = classic_factor(config=config, overlap=1.0, seed=10)
The resulting outcome, treatment, untreated-outcome, and effect matrices are numerically identical for the same seed and arguments.



Previous code configured arguments on each function call. Current code can create one reusable simulator:
simulator = classic_factor_design(config=config, overlap=1.0)

for panel in simulator.iter_simulations(200, seed=10):
    estimate = estimator.fit(*panel.as_arrays())
This uses spawned child streams and avoids coupling replication identifiers to adjacent integer seeds.



Previous canonical metadata was flat:
panel.metadata["factors"]
panel.metadata["loadings"]
Current metadata is namespaced by component:
panel.metadata["outcome"]["factors"]
panel.metadata["outcome"]["loadings"]
panel.metadata["assignment"]["treated_units"]
panel.metadata["effect"]["slope"]

The previous container set the write flag on supplied arrays. PanelDataset instead owns copies before making them read-only. Code that intentionally mutates estimator inputs must request copies:
y, w = panel.as_arrays(copy=True)



Custom designs no longer need to edit a canonical generator module. Implement an assignment, outcome, or effect protocol and compose it with PanelSimulator. Project-specific named designs can be stored in a DGPRegistry without changing the package registry.

title: Baker DGP: why vanilla TWFE event studies fail
text:
1 The failure design
Baker, Larcker, and Wang’s JFE replication contains a deliberately simple staggered-adoption design in Code/1g. Failures With Event Studies and Heterogeneity.R. Fifty state clusters are randomly divided into three adoption cohorts: 17 states adopt in 1989, 18 in 1998, and 15 in 2007. Cohort effects are positive and grow linearly after adoption, but their slopes decline from 0.10 to 0.05 to 0.01.
For unit \(i\) in cohort \(G_i=g\), pypanelsim implements
\[
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \varepsilon_{it}
       + W_{it}s_g(t-g+1),
\qquad
W_{it}=\mathbb{1}\{t\geq g\}.
\]
There are no anticipation effects and no structural pre-trends. Yet a vanilla relative-time TWFE regression combines valid not-yet-treated comparisons with comparisons that use already-treated units as controls. Because treatment effects differ across cohorts and event time, those comparisons contaminate one another.
The original code samples unit effects, time effects, and residuals from a private Compustat panel. The self-contained implementation uses centered Gaussian additive effects and errors instead. It preserves the part of the DGP that causes the failure: the calendar, randomized state cohorts, treatment timing, and dynamic cohort heterogeneity.

title: Baker DGP: why vanilla TWFE event studies fail
text:
2 Vanilla relative-time TWFE
We bin all leads before \(-6\) and lags after \(6\), omit event time \(-1\), and fit unit and period fixed effects with state-clustered standard errors. The executable PyFixest call is:


Show code
frame = baker_frame(panel, config)
window = 5
frame["event_time_binned"] = frame["rel_time"].clip(
    lower=-(window + 1), upper=window + 1
)

twfe_fit = pf.feols(
    "outcome ~ i(event_time_binned, ref=-1) | unit + time",
    frame,
    vcov={"CRV1": "state"},
)


This is the conventional event-study regression, not a cohort-specific design. The PyFixest difference-in-differences guide uses the same i(relative_time, ref=-1) | unit + year construction for a vanilla TWFE event study.

title: Baker DGP: why vanilla TWFE event studies fail
text:
3 Saturated cohort-by-event-time estimator
The correction fully interacts treatment cohort with event time, then aggregates the cohort-specific estimates using cohort shares. This is the saturated Sun–Abraham-style estimator exposed by PyFixest:


Show code
last_cohort = config.adoption_periods[-1]
saturated_frame = frame.loc[
    (frame["time"] < last_cohort)
    & ((frame["treatment"] == 0.0) | (frame["rel_time"] <= window))
].copy()
saturated_frame["cohort_for_estimator"] = saturated_frame["cohort_period"].mask(
    saturated_frame["cohort_period"] == last_cohort, 0
)

saturated_fit = pf.event_study(
    saturated_frame,
    yname="outcome",
    idname="unit",
    tname="time",
    gname="cohort_for_estimator",
    estimator="saturated",
    att=False,
    cluster="state",
)
